$$
\int 2(4x+2)^{-6}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=4x+2.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=4\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\text{d}u.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 2(4x+2)^{-6}\,\text{d}x & =(2)\int {u}^{-6}\cdot (\frac{1}{4})\,\text{d}u \\  & =(2)\cdot (\frac{1}{4})\int {u}^{-6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =(\frac{1}{2})\int {u}^{-6}\,\text{d}u \\  & =(\frac{1}{2})\cdot \frac{{u}^{-5}}{(-5)}+C \\  & =(- \frac{1}{10})(4x+2)^{-5}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{10(4x+2)^{5}}+C\end{aligned}

$$

First, we rewrite the integral as

$$
\int -4(10-5x)^{-7}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=10-5x.$ Then differentiating with respect to $x$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-5\,⟹\,\text{d}x=- \frac{1}{5}\text{d}u.
$$

We now write our integral in terms of $u,$ calculate the integral as normal, and write the final answer in terms of $x$ at the very end:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -4(10-5x)^{-7}\,\text{d}x & =(-4)\int {u}^{-7}\cdot (- \frac{1}{5})\,\text{d}u \\  & =(-4)\cdot (- \frac{1}{5})\int {u}^{-7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =(\frac{4}{5})\int {u}^{-7}\,\text{d}u \\  & =(\frac{4}{5})\cdot \frac{{u}^{-6}}{(-6)}+C \\  & =(- \frac{2}{15})(10-5x)^{-6}+C \\  & =-\frac{2}{15(10-5x)^{6}}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Let's double-check that our result is correct. If we differentiate the result, then it should come out to the original integrand:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{2}{15(10-5x)^{6}}+C] & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[-\frac{2}{15(10-5x)^{6}}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =(- \frac{2}{15})\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}[(10-5x)^{-6}]+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) \\  & =(- \frac{2}{15})\cdot (-6)\cdot (10-5x)^{-7}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(10-5x)+0 \\  & =(- \frac{2}{15})\cdot (-6)\cdot (10-5x)^{-7}\cdot (-5) \\  & =\frac{-4}{(10-5x)^{7}}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
